acts.title: Paper Can Hold a City
acts.summary: Trace the public network, meet the rival, and choose a route.

acts.title: Promises Need Addresses
acts.summary: Sort supplies, recover public tools, and name courier duties.

acts.title: The Click That Matters
acts.summary: Build a regulator, choose a supply policy, and verify the tests.

acts.title: A Boundary Worth Keeping
acts.summary: Inspect the lodge, choose a trust process, and secure a bypass.

acts.title: The Reply Comes Back
acts.summary: Design an independent signal path and test safe service.

acts.title: A Working Morning
acts.summary: Set duties, settle the real debt, choose an emphasis, and launch.

missions.title: The City in the Drawer
missions.summary: Find the missing public heat record.
intro: The desk came with your garage. So did a complaint: Frostwick keeps paying to thaw the same pipe. Now the city wants to sell the network. Pip would like one fact before they sign.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: speak to the clerk.
pages: Clerk: Aurora did not vanish. It was filed under Seasonal Mood. That drawer holds a tax appeal from a snowman. Search the catalog for SERVICE. The public repair ledger has a square seal; private sales use a crown.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: compare the dated index notes at the blueprint table.
pages: The table holds three index notes. December: repairs complete, signed by the engineer. January: sale proposed, unsigned. February: ownership unchanged until a deed is signed and entered. A resident named Mara needs to know who must fix her leaking stair pipe. She has already been sent between three desks. The clerk says a later date does not make an unsigned proposal into a completed transfer.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: choose the public service seal at the catalog.
pages: The catalog has three seal marks. Which mark identifies the public repair ledger? Use the filing rule the clerk gave you, rather than the most decorative cover.
wrong: Recall the clerk filing rule for public service. Sales and parties
have different marks.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: collect the badge at the badge stand.
pages: The badge is warm from the clerk holding it. Its owner was the last city pipe walker. A penciled note reads: If anyone says the network is dead, ask who stopped checking the valves.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: identify which record actually changed ownership.
pages: Mara asks whether the newer sale proposal means she must call a private estate office. Consider the dates, signatures, and the rule about entering a deed. Which conclusion can the clerk support? Pip will put it on her referral card and sign his name, so a confident guess could send her back into the cold.
wrong: Check the signature on the January proposal and the February rule. A
proposed event and a completed legal act need different evidence.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: show the badge to the foreman.
pages: Foreman: I knew that coat. Your aunt carried soup in the left pocket and drawings in the right. Sometimes the drawings smelled of leek. She left a manifest here, and a warning against people selling perfect winters.

outro: Pip writes: Network condition unknown. Fair. Nobody's checked it yet. The foreman offers a small records fee from the public repair fund. It's a start, and it pays.

missions.title: A Receipt for Winter
missions.summary: Trace the last delivery without buying anything.
intro: The depot's equipment sits idle. The kettle gets plenty of work. Aurora closed, but parts kept moving and someone kept signing the manifest. A neat silver S. Subtle.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: read the manifest board.
pages: Manifest: The red cart carried bells. The blue cart carried blankets. The yellow cart carried a pressure valve to Brassworks. Silver S signed for the yellow cart, then crossed out the destination. The carbon copy survived.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: compare the paid bill and storage tally beside the gate.
pages: The valve account shows twenty Coins for inspection, already paid by Slush, and six for storage, still disputed. The city claim slip keeps ownership public. The foreman remembers Slush paying promptly when the pipe was moved; he also remembers nobody agreeing to private ownership. Pip suggests thanking him for the actual payment without accepting the extra claim. The foreman hands you a clean tally card.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: inspect the toolbox for the carbon copy.
pages: Inside the toolbox is the carbon copy, folded around a biscuit. The valve was not sold. It was sent for inspection, with the city retaining ownership. Pip puts the biscuit back. Evidence should have standards.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: identify the valve cart at the gate.
pages: The gate register needs the color of the cart that carried the valve. Which exit slip should the clerk retrieve?
wrong: Match the valve cargo to its cart in the manifest, rather than
choosing the color of a different useful supply.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: prepare the factual account at the manifest board.
pages: The tally must separate a verified past payment from a disputed charge. Which amount can you truthfully record as already paid by Slush? This is not permission to take money from your wallet. It is the figure the foreman will acknowledge, and Slush will see whether you counted his contribution honestly.
wrong: The inspection and storage entries have different payment states.
Count only an entry marked paid, not every figure on the account.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: ask the foreman about the silver signature.
pages: Foreman: Sterling Slush paid the inspection bill. He may own the bill, but that is not the same as owning the valve. Tell the archive clerk we still know the difference. Tell Pip the kettle does not.

outro: The claim slip is protected from scrapping. Slush paid to keep something safe. That's useful. Whether he wants to save the network or own it is still unclear.

missions.title: The Map Under the Map
missions.summary: Choose the route you will defend.
intro: The new map shows five separate developments. The old one underneath connects them all. Pip wants to rip the top sheet off. The clerk hands him a sponge. Let's keep the evidence in one piece.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: lift the overlay at the blueprint table.
pages: The old route joins Frostwick Depot, Candy Sorting, Brassworks Control, Velvet Lodge, and Aurora Signal. The northern roof line reaches couriers quickly. The southern sheltered line keeps parcels dry. Both are public routes, despite the newer map.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: read the route capacity card at the antenna.
pages: Moxie has six small parcels for the first round. Her roof harness carries three at a time; the covered handcart carries all six. The high line is checked in two trips, and the covered line in one. Neither route has a timer. The clinic wants a complete delivery record, not a speed boast. Moxie asks how many trips the larger cart saves on this round.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: speak to the courier beside the roof landing.
pages: Moxie: I can take the high line. Three turns, excellent view, terrible hat insurance. The covered route serves the clinic. It is longer but gives me someone to talk to besides weather vanes. Pick a promise we can keep.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: choose a route at the weather vane.
pages: The vane bears two service marks: HIGH for the roof circuit, COVER for the sheltered clinic circuit. This sets your delivery plan. Both routes stay walkable, and the city will remember which promise you made.
outcomes: Moxie ties a bright roof ribbon. We will keep the roof stops
supplied, she says. Speed is useful when it has an address.
Moxie knots a rain cover onto the harness. The clinic gets a
dependable round. She calls it the dry victory and refuses to
explain the joke.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: compare trips for the six-parcel round.
pages: Use the capacity card to compare the six-parcel load. How many fewer trips does the covered handcart need than the roof harness? Your route choice remains valid either way: the answer tells Moxie how to staff it. A roof route can make two honest trips rather than claim an overloaded harness is somehow more festive.
wrong: Divide the six parcels by each carrying limit, then compare those
trip counts. Do not confuse the number of parcels with the number of
journeys.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: confirm the route with Moxie.
pages: Moxie pins your route on the sorting desk. She stops calling the project a rescue. Rescue sounds like one brave person, she says. A route needs somebody to do it again tomorrow. Pip quietly changes the heading.

outro: You've made a first public promise. The investigation will be here when you get back. Explore, take jobs, buy property if you want. A walk won't lose your place.

missions.title: The Wrong Kind of Sale
missions.summary: Separate a repair claim from a property claim.
intro: Nib's Velvet Lodge ad offers five districts to one owner. Nice trick, considering four properties aren't in the sale. Their shared pipe seems to be. The clerk has seen this one before.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: read the listing stand.
pages: Nib: The lodge boasts heated floors, a private horizon, and mature silence. The silence is actually a broken pump. I wrote the listing before I saw the pipe map. I would like to correct that before someone believes me.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: compare the invoice and sale schedule with Nib.
pages: Nib lays two pages side by side. The invoice names one valve inspection and six repaired roof panels. The sale schedule names the lodge walls and courtyard but excludes municipal pipes. A tempting summary says Slush paid for everything below the roof. Nib crosses it out. The inspection bill names a service, not a transfer of the inspected object. He asks for wording a nervous buyer could safely repeat.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: collect the disclosure from the disclosure desk.
pages: The disclosure lists walls, roof, and courtyard. It excludes municipal pipes and rights of passage. A separate inspection invoice carries Slush's letterhead. Nib circles EXCLUDES with a pen expensive enough to regret every circle.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: identify the document that governs the pipes.
pages: After comparing the disclosure with the inspection invoice, who retains the pipe network?
wrong: The property schedule excludes a kind of infrastructure. An
inspection payment proves a service, not a deed transfer.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: correct the listing claim using both pages.
pages: Which statement can stay on the corrected listing? Consider what the invoice proves was done and what the sale schedule actually includes. Slush will receive the revision too. Nib wants to acknowledge real repairs without turning an inspected public pipe into private property, or pretending a paid inspection was never useful work.
wrong: One page proves repairs were paid for; the other defines the
property. Reject both the inflated ownership claim and the claim
that nothing was done.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: meet Slush by the umbrella stand.
pages: Slush: You have discovered a distinction. Congratulations. I discovered twelve leaking roofs while the council discovered lunch. Bring me a workable network plan, and I will discuss my invoice. Bring me a slogan, and I will charge for the umbrella.

outro: Slush accepts the public claim. He doubts you can run it. Prove the routes, rebuild the regulator, name who answers a broken valve. Pip writes it down. Three things. Doable.

missions.title: Address Unknown, Soup Included
missions.summary: Sort the relief parcels using written clues.
intro: Candy Row has plenty of donated parcels. The labels are the problem. Moxie wants to try your route with one small delivery. These are city supplies, separate from your stock. No shopping required.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: read the address board.
pages: Address board: The clinic takes blankets, never bells. The roof watch takes bells, never food. Cocoa Corner takes the soup tin. Red shelf holds bells. Blue shelf holds blankets. The soup is already at the dispatch desk.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: ask Moxie about the handling requirements.
pages: A second shipment has a tin of soup and a packet of paper medicine labels. The clinic takes the labels and requires a dry container. Cocoa takes soup and can accept a washable crate. The only dry box holds the soup; the washable crate holds the labels. Both containers have correct address tags for their contents. Moxie says the tags are right but the packing still needs a decision.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: collect the blanket parcel from the blue shelf.
pages: The blue parcel has a stitched square and smells faintly of cedar. Inside the tag, a nurse has written: Thank you for sending things that fit actual people. Moxie checks the seal, then marks this as a protected delivery.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: label the red bell parcel.
pages: Choose the destination for the red shelf parcel. Use the contents and recipient rules on the address board, rather than the color alone.
wrong: Look up what the red shelf holds, then match that item with the
recipient that requested it.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: choose a packing action that preserves both destinations.
pages: Which action meets both handling needs without changing who receives either item? The address tags can move with their contents. Nothing is spoiled yet, and there is no hurry. A correct delivery means checking the parcel as well as the name on it. Moxie waits with the dispatch pen instead of rewarding the first answer.
wrong: The clinic labels must stay dry. Compare the two containers, then
ask which change preserves the correct destinations while fixing the
handling problem.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: give the route plan to the courier.
pages: Moxie: The point is that each parcel has a reason to be on the cart. We are not making the city look supplied. We are supplying it. She keeps the spare label in case someone tries to send the clinic a decorative gong.
Moxie: Your high route gets the watch bell first. A fast alarm can
help the sheltered streets too.
Moxie: Your covered route protects the blankets first. The watch
agreed to wait its proper turn.

outro: Right parcels, right people. Moxie marks the board. There was no timer to beat; reading the labels did more good than running would have.

missions.title: Wind Has No Forwarding Address
missions.summary: Recover the roof signal records.
intro: The roof bell rang when Aurora failed. The station heard nothing. Slush blames shared systems. Dot, standing behind a chimney, asks if anyone checked the wire. Nobody answers immediately.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: inspect the antenna terminal.
pages: Dot: The bell wire goes to this antenna. Its brass tag says SEND NORTH. The vane points toward Aurora when its arrow meets the notch. Wind moved the vane, but the notch is still cut into the stone.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: compare the dated watch entries with the courier.
pages: Three entries survive in the watch log. At seven, the roof sent its alarm. At eight, Aurora recorded that alarm. At nine, Aurora attempted a reply, but no roof receipt was logged. Dot points out that the first two entries show a successful outward path. A later problem may affect the return path without erasing the earlier delivery. The watch keeper wants his crew cleared of a false accusation.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: recover the sealed parcel chest.
pages: A waxed parcel holds the watch log, kept dry beneath the chest lid. The alarm was sent. The acknowledgment never came back. Dot reads this twice, then asks you to carry the original while she keeps an exact copy.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: align the signal vane using its brass tag.
pages: Align the vane for the signal destination named on the antenna tag. Which direction matches its fixed stone mark?
wrong: The movable arrow is not a reliable landmark in wind. Compare the
antenna instruction with the fixed notch.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: locate the first unconfirmed signal leg.
pages: Which leg needs investigation first: the alarm leaving the roof, the alarm reaching Aurora, or the attempted reply returning? Use the separate entries rather than assuming the whole system either worked or failed. The watch keeper has waited years to hear an answer that distinguishes what his crew did from what the machinery could confirm.
wrong: Find the earliest missing confirmation. Two entries record completed
events; the third records an attempt without its receiving mark.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: show the watch log to the signal clerk.
pages: Clerk: We received the bell. We sent a reply through the same wire after the relay froze. That reply never left the building. Two messages, one wire, and no other way to ask for help. Dot shuts her notebook very softly.

outro: One frozen link cut everyone off, even though they'd done their jobs. Dot wants a second path before a bigger bell. Pip adds her name to the plan. She earned the space.

missions.title: The Sled Is Not the Debt
missions.summary: Recover public equipment through its records.
intro: The depot has a repossessed service sled. Slush paid its storage, then a clerk marked it as collateral. Moxie used to drive it. The left runner still owes her an apology.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: recover the sled register from the address board.
pages: The sled register lists the city as owner. Its repair charge was paid from a public fund. Storage is the only unpaid item. A penciled note says equipment cannot be pledged by a driver. Moxie looks deeply relieved by this detail.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: inspect the sled release checklist at the gate.
pages: The release checklist requires two facts: public ownership and a cleared repair charge. The sorting register proves ownership; the paid repair line proves the charge cleared. The storage dispute belongs on a separate account. A substitute form offers release if Moxie signs a personal loan. She could sign quickly, but it would turn a public paperwork error into her private debt. She puts the pen down.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: compare the sled entry on the manifest.
pages: Manifest: Vehicle loan: none. Repair debt: cleared. Storage claim: disputed. Release requires the municipal owner mark, a square. The crown stamp would transfer a private vehicle, which this sled has never been.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: select the lawful release mark at the gate.
pages: Select the release form appropriate to this sled ownership. The mark is specified in the manifest.
wrong: Decide whether the vehicle is public or private, then use the
corresponding release mark named by the manifest.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: choose the evidence packet for a fair sled release.
pages: Which packet satisfies the two release conditions without making Moxie personally liable? The clerk can attach more than one document. Do not solve a missing proof by inventing a new borrower. Moxie says she will wait while you get it right; the sled belongs to the city, and so does the duty to keep its records straight.
wrong: The checklist has two required facts. A single register proves only
one of them; a personal loan creates a new obligation instead of
proving the old facts.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: report the sled release to Moxie.
pages: Moxie: We can use the sled again without pretending the storage bill disappeared. That is a surprisingly grown up victory. She writes REPAIR THE RUNNER before drawing a racing stripe. The stripe comes second, by a narrow vote.

outro: Moxie takes care of the released sled and its courier work. You get the signed receipt. The disputed bill still exists; getting a tool back didn't magically pay it.

missions.title: A Promise With a Roof
missions.summary: Make the first route accountable.
intro: Pip's launch speech says boundless. Moxie crosses that out. The route has stops, limits, and a weak bridge. Check the survey and name who's responsible before anyone makes a speech.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: read the survey desk.
pages: Survey: The west service bridge bears parcels, not machinery. The east stair bears a hand cart. Heavy regulator parts must travel by depot gate. Nib asks whether describing the bridge as intimate would help. Rivet answers without looking up.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: compare load and route limits on the dispatch board.
pages: The regulator crate weighs six units. The west roof bridge holds three. The east stair holds five. The depot gate holds eight. The crate must travel intact because its spring is secured inside a sealed test frame. Moxie cannot split it into two trips without invalidating the test. The gate route is longer on the drawing but has no toll, timer, or closed door.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: choose the safe path for heavy parts.
pages: Which route did the survey approve for the heavy regulator parts? Choose a route that respects its load limits.
wrong: The survey distinguishes parcel routes from the machinery route.
Shorter does not mean strong enough.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: agree the route duty with the courier.
pages: Moxie: I will keep the stop list and log a missed call. Pip will answer when I report one. Nobody gets to replace the word missed with almost. The roof watch volunteers a dry shelf for the log.
The watch keeps your high circuit first on its board. Moxie notes
the wind check beside each roof stop.
The clinic keeps your covered circuit first on its board. Moxie adds
a dry bag check beside its stop.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: approve the intact regulator route on the survey.
pages: After routing the intact crate through the suitable gate, how many weight units of capacity remain on that crossing? The limits are maximum loads, not targets that must be filled. Moxie wants to know whether a one-unit hand tool bag can accompany the crate without breaking the limit. Count the crate first, then find the remaining margin.
wrong: Subtract the intact crate weight from the selected gate capacity.
Capacity remaining is different from the total capacity printed on
the gate.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: sign the dispatch promise with Moxie.
pages: Pip reads his smaller speech: We will visit these stops, record what fails, and tell people the truth. Moxie signs it. Dot signs as witness. Nib says it lacks sparkle, then asks for a copy to hang in the lodge.

outro: Candy Row has named duties and a route plan. You didn't need to buy the sorting house. Next comes the regulator. Rivet looks relieved to be dealing with parts.

missions.title: The Last Honest Gear
missions.summary: Find the regulator parts and their actual purpose.
intro: The regulator's old guard took its cage home for a greenhouse. Rivet kept the parts on shelves. Before she builds anything, she'd like to know you understand what it's for. Reasonable request.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: ask Rivet about the regulator.
pages: Rivet: A gear moves the valve. A spring pulls it shut when power fails. A brass key sets the limit. None is optional. The old machine had a marvelous opening motion and a closing spring borrowed to fix a musical chair.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: compare the two spring tags on the shelf.
pages: Rivet has two springs. The short spring closes a valve that travels two marks. The long spring closes one that travels four. This regulator travels four marks and must close fully with power off. Both springs look clean. A trainee chose the short one because it fits the tin more neatly. Rivet asks you to explain the selection without making the trainee afraid to ask another question.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: collect the tagged gears.
pages: The gears turn freely in Rivet's gloves. Each tooth has a number rather than a decorative snowflake. She says decorative snowflakes are acceptable on many things, including neither load teeth nor safety instructions. Dot copies the numbers into the parts record.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: recover the spring and limit key from the shelf.
pages: The spring sits inside a biscuit tin marked DO NOT EAT ENGINEERING. The brass key hangs beside it. Rivet checks both against her drawing. Rivet tags the parts for public repair and locks their carrying case. Whatever you build for yourself, these belong to the network.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: select the spring that matches the full valve travel.
pages: Which spring belongs in the regulator test frame? Judge it by the required closing travel, not by polish or how well it stores. Rivet will ask the trainee to repeat your reason before fitting it. A useful correction should leave the next builder understanding the part, rather than merely remembering that a senior person preferred it.
wrong: Match the valve travel to the spring rating. A spring that closes
only part of the required distance cannot provide the full safe
action.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: select the part that closes the valve on failure.
pages: Which regulator part supplies the closing action when power fails?
wrong: Rivet assigned a different job to each part. Find the job that
remains possible with the power disconnected.

outro: You bring Rivet all the parts and a correct answer. That's enough for her to oversee a test. Pip nearly says miracle worker. Chief builder will do.

missions.title: Enough Is a Setting
missions.summary: Choose a supply policy with a real later effect.
intro: You've got the regulator parts. Now pick a repair policy: hold a reserve for faults, or share batches with a public parts ledger. Neither uses your workshop salvage today. This is about the next shortage.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: read Dot's test notes.
pages: Dot: One standard batch makes two seals from two units. One repair takes one seal. The next inspection needs two seals. So a single batch covers that inspection exactly. A second batch is a buffer, not a requirement we should hide.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: inspect the two batch recipes on the pump desk.
pages: Rivet presents a DIFFERENT practice order, separate from the two-seal standard inspection. This order needs exactly three seals, with no spare output because the mix expires. Six stock units are available; two must remain for another crew. Recipe A uses two stock for two seals. Recipe B uses four stock for three. Only whole batches are allowed. The first standard inspection and this practice order must each be planned on their own terms.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: plan the inspection batch count.
pages: For the original standard inspection, use Dot two-seal requirement and the standard two-seal batch, not the different practice recipes. How many standard batches cover that inspection exactly before adding a buffer?
wrong: Compare the inspection need with the output of a single standard
batch. Extra capacity is not part of the stated requirement.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: choose the repair supply policy with Rivet.
pages: Rivet offers RESERVE, holding spare seals for sudden faults, or SHARED, pooling orders and publishing the stock ledger. Each can work if people keep the promise. Choose the policy the crew will use in later tests.
outcomes: Rivet marks a spare shelf and gives Dot its inventory card. A
reserve only works if everyone knows what is truly there.
Rivet opens the batch ledger to every district. Shared stock only
works if an order is recorded before anyone counts on it.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: choose a whole-batch plan for the exact seal order.
pages: Which recipe plan meets all three constraints: exactly three seals, no partial batch, and at least two stock left? Read the output as carefully as the input. Two small batches may look economical until you count what they make. The other crew has already planned a repair around the stock you promised not to consume.
wrong: Check both stock remaining and seal output for each plan. The order
requires an exact quantity, so extra output is not a free advantage.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: watch Rivet fit the regulator.
pages: The spring closes the valve with a small click. Rivet repeats the test with the power disconnected. The same click answers. Pip says it sounds less grand than expected. Rivet says good safety equipment often has excellent manners.

outro: The regulator is ready. Its parts belong to the public repair crew; your stock stays yours. The policy will matter when supplies run short. Rivet removes the musical chair from the queue. Wrong spring.

missions.title: The Needle That Lied
missions.summary: Calibrate the gauge against independent evidence.
intro: The gauge says pressure is healthy. The hose beside it isn't connected to anything. Pip admires the optimism. Dot suggests a bucket test. Rivet hands her a bucket.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: inspect the pump test card.
pages: Test card: With pump OFF, the open line must read ZERO. With pump ON, the measured bucket should fill to TWO marks. A gauge that reads TWO while the pump is off has a stuck needle, not secret pressure.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: read Dot independent check of the bucket marks.
pages: Dot tests the bucket itself before blaming the gauge. A certified jug pours one unit to its first mark and another unit to its second. The bucket agrees on both. The open line is visibly empty when the pump is off. A spare gauge from a private showroom has no test record. Slush offers it anyway, then listens when Dot explains that a more expensive reading is not independent evidence.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: compare the gauge and bucket.
pages: Dot turns the pump off. The line is open, the bucket is empty, and the needle still reads TWO. She records all three facts before touching the screw. Rivet says a neat notebook is less expensive than a neat explanation afterward.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: report the fault at the relay desk.
pages: Which fault explains the disagreement between the gauge and the physical checks?
wrong: Compare the off pump, open line, empty bucket, and needle claim.
Which observation fails to agree with the others?

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: choose the first justified corrective action.
pages: Which action follows the combined checks? The bucket agrees with the certified jug, the off line is empty, and the fixed needle claims pressure. You may inspect the gauge mechanism, replace the verified bucket, or raise pump power until the display looks right. Dot will record the reason before anyone touches a tool.
wrong: Look for the observation that disagrees with two separately checked
facts. Changing a verified reference or forcing the machine to match
a display would hide the disagreement.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: approve Dot's calibrated reading.
pages: With the needle freed, OFF reads ZERO. ON fills the bucket to TWO marks, and the gauge agrees. Dot signs the test herself. Pip offers a gold star. She accepts a second witness signature instead, then asks for the star as well.

outro: The reading now has a measured result behind it. Dot says the reply needs its own test, separate from the alarm. Rivet lets her finish. Dot stops staring at her shoes.

missions.title: A Shift Without Guesswork
missions.summary: Plan a safe sequence for building and testing.
intro: Slush's inspector brings a silver ruler to Brassworks. Rivet agrees the process needs checking. First, she moves his ruler away from the live contacts with a wooden spoon. Good opening lesson.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: inspect the process cards on the shelf.
pages: Process cards: FIT spring before energizing. SET limit after fitting. TEST with power last. Card order is not a suggestion. The inspector asks if the wooden spoon is approved equipment. Rivet says it is approved for moving his ruler.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: review the maintenance lock card with Dot.
pages: The lock card adds a condition to the process sheets: the crew must disconnect power before opening the regulator cover. The spring is fitted with the cover open. The limit is set after the spring is secured. The cover is then shut before power returns for testing. Dot arranges blank cards on the desk and asks the inspector to keep his silver ruler away from all of them.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: choose the safe process order.
pages: Which pair of actions must be completed, in that order, before the powered test?
wrong: Use the process cards prerequisites. One preparation action depends
on another; a test is necessary later but is not the preparation
pair.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: review the supply response at the relay.
pages: The inspector asks what happens if one seal fails the test. Rivet points to the supply promise you made, then asks Dot to explain how the replacement reaches the bench.
Dot: The labeled reserve shelf holds the replacement. I record its
use and request a new seal before calling the reserve full again.
Dot: The shared ledger assigns a spare from the next pooled batch. I
record the transfer so two districts cannot promise the same seal.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: choose the missing first action in the maintenance plan.
pages: The inspector has written OPEN, FIT, SET, CLOSE, TEST. Something must happen before OPEN, and must remain in force through the open-cover work. Which first action makes this sequence safe? This is a planning check, not a live switch experiment. Rivet will not open the machine until the written order accounts for the lock card.
wrong: The lock card governs work with the cover open. Find the power state
required before that work begins, rather than treating the later
test as the first task.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: receive the signed test record from Rivet.
pages: The inspector watches three cycles, including a loss of power. The valve closes each time. He signs a plain sheet. Slush wanted a certificate suitable for a wall. Rivet wants a record suitable for the next person at the bench.

outro: The regulator is tested and the operating order is written down. The inspector takes Slush a copy. Rivet lends him a coat and writes that down too. She wants the coat back.

missions.title: Open House, Open File
missions.summary: Read what the charming listing leaves out.
intro: Nib has arranged a tour of Velvet Lodge. The listing has three fewer adjectives. He's taking it hard. Slush has a real concern: the lodge floors sit over the main junction.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: begin the inspection with Nib.
pages: Nib: The west salon is called the Winter Room because winter enters it. I used to call that seasonal airflow. Now I am calling a roofer. The junction door is behind the listing stand, and the easement is in the disclosure.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: inspect the room footprints on the listing plan.
pages: The listing plan shows the service door south, the guest bedroom north, and the kitchen east. A repair crew can carry tools from the south door straight to the junction along the service hall. A proposed shortcut crosses the bedroom. Nib points to the easement: permission to repair pipes does not grant whatever route is shortest. A tenant has asked that workers stop treating her carpet as public infrastructure.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: collect the easement copy at the disclosure desk.
pages: The easement permits city workers to cross the service hall for pipe repairs. It does not grant public use of bedrooms or kitchen. The lodge owner keeps those rooms. Nib reads the boundary aloud, unusually free of theatrical gestures.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: mark the lawful access area on the listing.
pages: Which space does the easement authorize the repair crew to use?
wrong: The easement gives a specific service route and explicitly leaves
other rooms private. A destination does not grant every possible
approach.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: choose an access plan that respects the recorded boundary.
pages: Which instruction belongs in the crew access notice? Keep the service right effective without turning it into a claim over private rooms. The tenant will receive the same notice as the builders. Nib wants her to know exactly where strangers will walk, not merely be reassured that everyone means well and carries clean boots.
wrong: Trace the route that stays within the service hall. A shortcut is
not authorized merely because it reaches a permitted destination.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: inspect the junction behind the service door.
pages: Four branches feed into one iron throat. A polished brass wheel closes all four together. Dot sees fresh grease on the wheel. Someone has cared for it. Someone has also made every branch depend on a single moving piece.

outro: You can reach the public pipes. You can't take over the lodge. Nib puts that in the pitch, using fewer words than usual. The clerk can finally file it.

missions.title: Sterling, Before the Silver
missions.summary: Ask why Slush built a closed plan.
intro: Slush waits on the roof with a survey book under his umbrella. He's spent years paying for patches while the council argued. You can see why he's tired. The eviction plan still needs explaining.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: hear Slush's account of the failure.
pages: Slush: My father ran the east greenhouse. One frozen reply wire, one unopened valve, and a season of seedlings lost. The city sent condolences printed on very warm paper. I bought the lodge to stop waiting for permission to keep people safe.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: compare public review fields with the privacy note.
pages: The review file has four fields: repair amount, work date, tenant name, and medical note. The public fund needs the amount and work date to verify the repair. Neither a tenant name nor a medical note is needed for that check. Slush fears the review will make his residents into exhibits. Dot says accountability for money does not require exposing details that cannot prove how a roof was repaired.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: examine the greenhouse survey book.
pages: The survey lists actual repair costs, loans, and tenants who paid nothing during the freeze. Beside them is a future rent plan for the sealed district. It would fund maintenance, but half the current residents could not afford to remain.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: choose how to review Slush's repair records.
pages: Slush offers the full inspection file. You may REVIEW it together at his desk or request a PUBLIC review with the clerk. Both preserve his private tenant names. Choose the trust process for the negotiation.
outcomes: You agree to read the file with Slush before publishing findings. He
sets down the umbrella, an oddly serious gesture. Dot keeps an
independent copy of every test.
You ask the clerk to witness the review and publish its costs. Slush
objects to an audience, then accepts the rule that tenant names stay
private.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: select the version fit for the public repair review.
pages: Choose the public review copy: ALL includes every field; COSTS includes repair amount AND work date; NAMES includes tenant identities only. Which copy verifies the repair without exposing unrelated private details? Nib will compare it with the original before posting. Slush waits without suggesting that privacy should excuse hiding the price of the work. The same standard applies to either review process.
wrong: Keep the fields required to verify the repair, and omit personal
fields that do not establish the amount or date of the work.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: read the permit limits.
pages: Permit note: A private owner may maintain the junction but cannot shut public branches to reserve heat for a new estate. Slush signs beneath it. I know what the paper says, he tells Nib. I need to know the machine will agree.

outro: Slush agrees to a measured trial. His worry makes sense; evicting people still doesn't. Nib promises clear terms on one page. Everyone would appreciate seeing that.

missions.title: The Pages That Stayed Put
missions.summary: Resolve the permit packet by its evidence.
intro: The permit office blames wind for three missing pages. Dot spots them under the skylight latch. Nib fetches a long hook. Apparently we've reached the special equipment portion of finding paper.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: recover the permit packet at the skylight.
pages: The packet stays dry in a tin sleeve. Page ONE defines the service hall. Page TWO grants pipe access. Page THREE forbids closing public branches for private priority. Its seal matches the archive square, not Slush's silver stationery.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: compare the unsigned summary with Slush sealed permit pages.
pages: An estate summary says the lodge may reserve all heat after paying an inspection invoice. Page TWO grants service access, not ownership. Page THREE forbids closing public branches for private priority. The summary is unsigned; both numbered pages carry the city seal. Nib recognizes his old phrasing in the summary and admits he repeated a claim he had not checked. He asks to correct it where everyone can see.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: compare the permit pages at the permit board.
pages: Nib: The signature page refers to TWO for the access right. THREE limits how that right may be used. The clerk needs the access page first, then its limit. I could turn this into a speech. I am choosing to turn it into a packet.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: hand Nib the page granting pipe access.
pages: Which numbered page establishes the right to enter for pipe repairs?
wrong: Distinguish the definition of the space, the grant of access, and
the limit on private priority. Their functions are different.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: choose the correction for the unsupported permit summary.
pages: Which claim should replace the unsigned priority sentence? The signed pages still give useful repair access, so the correction must not erase that right. Compare what each document permits, and let the sealed terms govern the summary. Nib will put his name beneath the correction, including the uncomfortable sentence that the earlier claim was his mistake.
wrong: The valid pages grant a limited right and restrict its use. Reject
both an expanded private privilege and the opposite claim that no
access exists.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: read the posted access agreement at the junction.
pages: The clerk posts the packet beside the wheel. Private rooms remain private; public service stays public. Slush asks for clear fault reports in return. Pip accepts the duty and names Moxie as the person who will carry reports if a wire fails.

outro: The agreement allows access without buying the property. Nib leaves the hook by the door: FOR PAPER, NOT HEROICS. For once, his wording needs no edits.

missions.title: The Second Door
missions.summary: Make a bypass plan that respects the lodge.
intro: The junction still depends on one wheel. Rivet can add a bypass through the service hall, clear of private rooms. Dot checked the survey twice. Slush would like the route settled before the holes.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: read Dot's bypass survey.
pages: Survey: The north wall borders a bedroom. The east wall borders the kitchen. The south service wall meets the public pipe chase. Only the SOUTH path reaches the chase entirely within the recorded service easement. The old hatch is already there.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: inspect the bypass work card at the skylight.
pages: The south chase has two fitting positions. Position A needs a new hole through a private kitchen wall. Position B uses the existing service hatch and costs one extra elbow joint. Both stay within the pressure rating, and the city fund covers either joint count. The signed permission covers only the existing hatch. Rivet says a cheaper pipe does not become cheaper if it buys an argument with a tenant.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: select the bypass wall at the junction.
pages: Which existing hatch reaches the pipe chase without entering a private room?
wrong: Trace each surveyed wall to the room or chase beyond it. Only a
route within the recorded easement is already authorized.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: present the bypass plan to Slush.
pages: Slush checks the line with his own ruler. The second door does not remove his wheel. It prevents his wheel from being the only door. He asks Dot to explain what fails if the bypass freezes too.
Slush: We read the file together. Your plan names the same faults I
did and proposes an answer I can check. That earns a trial, not
blind faith.
Slush: The clerk published my costs accurately. I disliked the
process. I have less reason to distrust its drawing. Let the witness
keep the test log.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: approve the fitting that matches the signed permission.
pages: Which fitting position is ready to authorize under the agreement you already hold? Neither option needs your personal money. The decision is about matching work to its legal and physical boundary. Slush can grant a new kitchen-wall agreement later if the tenant consents, but that permission does not exist now and should not be assumed.
wrong: Compare each position with the actual signed permission. A
technically safe design can still require an access right the crew
has not obtained.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: receive the signed bypass permission at the disclosure desk.
pages: Nib reads every limit before anyone signs. The permission covers the existing hatch and pipe chase only. Slush adds his repair invoice as a separate attachment. For once, nobody tries to sell a corridor by calling it a lifestyle.

outro: Velvet has a lawful bypass route and a test agreement. Aurora is next. Moxie maps both roof circuits. Slush offers Rivet a better desk lamp. She could actually use one.

missions.title: Where the Reply Went
missions.summary: Diagnose the signal failure without blaming the sender.
intro: Aurora Signal smells of old varnish and unclaimed tea. The clerk has kept the failure log for years, waiting for someone to ask. She's glad you're here. She's also going to mention the wait.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: collect the signal log at the box.
pages: Log: Roof alarm received. Station reply sent. Shared relay froze before the reply left. No second path existed. The operator stayed to hand carry the reply, but the gate crew had already withdrawn. Nobody could confirm whether the message arrived.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: study the two-fault map drill with the clerk.
pages: Dot marks a second paper fault: the depot gate is blocked while the relay remains frozen. Courier route A crosses that gate. Foot route B goes through the archive service lane and touches neither gate nor relay. Wire route C uses the frozen relay. These are test marks only; no public doorway is locked. Moxie asks for a backup that survives both faults, not just the one that made yesterday famous.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: inspect the message paths on the map.
pages: Dot: The wire path runs roof, relay, station. A courier path can run station, depot, roof. They share no relay. A second wire through the same frozen box would have the same fault. A new color is not a new path.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: select the independent backup at the lantern.
pages: For the EARLIER relay-only failure, before the gate fault was added, which backup avoided the failed relay? The next check will separately ask you to solve the two-fault drill. Keep the two cases distinct in the log.
wrong: A backup must avoid the failed component. Changing the appearance of
a path while keeping its dependency does not make it independent.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: choose the message path that avoids both marked faults.
pages: For this two-fault drill, which route can still carry the reply? Use the map topology rather than assuming any courier path must be independent. Moxie is willing to walk the longer foot route, but wants the planner to name why it is needed. Dot keeps both blocked components marked so nobody forgets the second constraint while solving the first.
wrong: Trace each path against both marked failures. A route is independent
only if it avoids every component the drill has taken out.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: give the clerk the independent path plan.
pages: Clerk: I will log the sent message and ask for a received mark. If no mark returns, Moxie carries a copy. We will not call silence agreement. Pip writes that sentence at the top, then asks permission to keep it there.

outro: Dot writes the rule down. The clerk gives her the good pencil, barely longer than its eraser. Dot uses it to label the backup path. No need to save it for an occasion.

missions.title: A Light With a Meaning
missions.summary: Agree on a signal people can actually read.
intro: The festival committee proposed seven lantern signals. The clerk crossed out six. A warning needs to make sense to someone cold, worried, and wearing mittens. Seven is asking a lot.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: learn the lantern code from the clerk.
pages: Clerk: STEADY means message received. DOUBLE means send the courier. DARK means no confirmed signal, so check in person. No rapid flashing, and no color test. We use a plain written card at every post as well as the lamp.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: inspect the damaged-card drill beside the map.
pages: A sample report says someone saw a lamp but could not tell whether it was steady or double. The receiver must not invent a clear code from an unclear sighting. A written received card at the post can resolve the doubt; if it cannot, the receiver must check in person. The clerk remembers how much trouble began when silence was treated as agreement. An uncertain flash deserves the same honest caution.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: collect the written signal card at the lantern.
pages: The card uses words and distinct marks. Pip can read it at arm length; Moxie can read it through a scarf. Nib proposes a gold border. The clerk permits the border after he proves it covers none of the instructions.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: answer the double signal at the antenna.
pages: The roof antenna receives a clear DOUBLE signal. What action does the agreed code require?
wrong: Consult the signal card. Receipt confirmation, backup request, and
lack of a confirmed signal each have a distinct response.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: choose the response to an uncertain lamp report.
pages: What should the roof keeper do first with a report that cannot distinguish the two active signals? The written received card is available beside the lamp. No warning is currently confirmed. Choose a check that can establish what was actually sent before calling either receipt or a courier request. The keeper wants a rule that still works on a misty night.
wrong: An uncertain observation is not a known signal. Use the available
independent written record before assigning a meaning to the light.

steps.hint: Candy Rooftops: confirm the backup duty with Moxie.
pages: Moxie repeats the signal and names the depot handoff. She asks Pip to stop calling her the emergency miracle. A courier is a normal part of the plan, she says. Miracles have terrible maintenance schedules.
Your high route makes the roof watch the first backup contact. Moxie
also sends the clinic a written copy by the depot.
Your covered route makes the clinic the first handoff. Moxie
continues to the roof watch with the matching written copy.

outro: The signal has a meaning, a reply, and a backup around the old fault. You followed the agreed rule. No waiting period or reflex test needed. The crew records the choice.

missions.title: Pressure Is Not a Vote
missions.summary: Set the limit from a measured safe range.
intro: Aurora Core is bigger than Pip expected. Rivet likes how quiet it is. The turbine plate lists safe, test, and maximum marks. Slush once treated the last one as a daily target. Let's check the plate.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: inspect the turbine plate.
pages: Rivet: The measured safe service limit is FOUR. SIX is a brief test ceiling, not a normal setting. EIGHT is a damage warning. We set the regulator for service, then verify the gauge. Bigger is not a plan just because it fits on a sign.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: read the branch demand card at the bypass.
pages: The first service plan has four pressure units available within the safe limit. The clinic needs two, the depot needs one, and the foundry needs one. A decorative steam arch would take another two. The arch is optional; the three working stops are not. Pip admits he drew the arch before adding the demand numbers. Rivet hands him an eraser without commenting on its impressive curve.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: collect Dot's signed service setting card.
pages: Dot checks the bucket record against the turbine plate. FOUR remains the safe service limit. She signs the card and asks Rivet to witness it. Slush watches the two signatures and asks where to put his. Dot gives him the copy receipt.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: set the safe service limit at the grid.
pages: Choose the normal service setting from the signed engineering record.
wrong: The plate distinguishes daily service, a brief test ceiling, and a
damage warning. Only one category applies to normal operation.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: approve a launch load that fits the measured service budget.
pages: Which launch plan serves every required stop without exceeding the measured limit? The choice of future emphasis does not add pressure today. Slush offers to buy brighter paint for the arch instead. You must decide whether it can run now, not whether it would photograph well or whether someone can afford its construction.
wrong: Add the required branch demands first. Compare their total with the
available safe service, then test whether optional demand still
fits.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: review the isolation plan at the bypass.
pages: Rivet shows separate branch valves. A blocked district can be isolated while the others keep service. The bypass does not create more heat. It gives the crew a way to make a repair without making the whole city wait outside.

outro: The core is within its measured limit. Pip erases UNLIMITED. Slush admits his estate drawing used the test ceiling, and listens while Dot corrects it. That part is new.

missions.title: The Fault We Invited
missions.summary: Test a branch failure before trusting the launch.
intro: For the trial, the crew marks the lodge branch shut on paper. No damage, no lost service. Work out the response before a real cold night. Slush agrees to leave his wheel alone.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: read the staged fault card at the bypass.
pages: Fault card: Lodge branch closed. Frostwick, Candy, and Brassworks branches clear. The independent bypass is open. Correct response: isolate the closed lodge branch, keep clear branches served, and send the lodge a fault report. Closing everything repeats the old failure.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: compare the staged leak measurements with Dot.
pages: The drill adds measured demand: clear branches need three units together. The faulty lodge branch leaks two extra units. Safe service is four. Isolating the lodge removes the leak and leaves the clear branches at three. Raising the service setting to six would hide the shortage without repairing the fault, and six is still only a test ceiling. Slush checks the arithmetic himself and does not like how familiar the wrong plan feels.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: choose the response to the lodge fault.
pages: What response follows the staged branch fault plan?
wrong: Only one branch has a fault. Consider whether the independent bypass
can keep the clear branches operating while that fault is contained.

steps.hint: Brassworks Control: record how the supply policy covers the repair.
pages: The paper test calls for one replacement seal at Velvet. Rivet asks the crew to show the stock entry and name the replenishment duty before calling the repair supplied.
The reserve card assigns one spare to Velvet and marks it used. Pip
logs a replacement request. The reserve does its job without
pretending it stayed full.
The shared ledger transfers one seal from the pooled batch to
Velvet. Candy sees the update, so nobody counts that seal twice. The
next shared order replaces it.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: select the safe response to the measured leak drill.
pages: After isolating the leaking lodge branch, how many service units remain as headroom while all clear branches stay supplied? This margin is not permission to raise the regulator. It shows whether the chosen response fits the measured safe limit. Slush wants the number written beside the operating instruction so a future crew can see why it was safe.
wrong: Use the clear-branch demand after the leak is isolated. Subtract
that demand from the safe service limit, rather than counting the
leak as a working branch.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: review the fault result with Slush.
pages: Slush: My plan protected one district by excluding the rest. Yours keeps the rest served while admitting one needs help. That is a distinction with a machine behind it. He signs the trial result and asks to keep the paper fault card.

outro: One blocked branch doesn't have to stop the clear ones. That's what this trial showed. Slush accepts it. Pip leaves out the part of his speech where nothing ever goes wrong again.

missions.title: Who Holds the Spare Key
missions.summary: Write down the duties before the ribbon.
intro: The festival committee brings a lot of ribbon. Nib asks them to wait. First, someone has to take responsibility for the spare keys. The committee puts the scissors down.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: review the duty register with the clerk.
pages: Register: Rivet maintains valves. Dot verifies readings. Moxie carries failed message copies. Pip records faults and informs residents. The clerk keeps the public access agreement. Slush offers his roof crew for lodge repairs, subject to the same written fault log.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: review the duty handoff example with the clerk.
pages: A resident reports a cold room but the current gauge reading is unverified. Pip must acknowledge the resident and record the report. Dot checks the reading. Rivet decides the mechanical repair from verified evidence. Moxie carries a copy if the signal reply fails. One draft skips straight from complaint to ordering Rivet to replace the pump. The clerk asks who has been left out, and why that omission matters.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: assign the missing reply at the signal box.
pages: A message has no received mark. Who is assigned to carry its backup copy?
wrong: Read the duty register as separate jobs. Measuring and repairing do
not replace the person assigned to carry a failed message.

steps.hint: Velvet Lodge: settle the invoice terms with Nib.
pages: Nib reads the proposed settlement: verified repair costs are repaid from the public fund in recorded installments. No tenant loses a home to pay it. Slush gives up the sealed estate priority. The city takes an actual debt, not a flattering favor.
The joint review kept Slush's private tenant notes out of the
settlement. Dot verified the repair sums separately; the clerk
publishes only the agreed totals.
The witnessed public review publishes the repair totals and test
records. Tenant names remain private. Slush signs beneath the same
figures the clerk checked.

steps.hint: Frostwick Archive: correct the missing handoff in the duty example.
pages: Before choosing a mechanical replacement, whose assigned work must occur in the example? The resident report is real and should be acknowledged. It does not by itself identify which part failed. Choose the missing verification handoff, so the duty register protects both the resident from delay and the builder from repairing a guess.
wrong: Find the named duty that checks whether the reading is trustworthy.
Reporting a symptom and deciding which part to replace are different
steps.

steps.hint: Velvet Rooftops: receive Slush's signed settlement.
pages: Slush: I still prefer a building with my name on it. But a city that works is a better neighbor than an estate surrounded by cold. He offers the umbrella to Pip, who discovers it is heavy because the handle stores twelve emergency forms.

outro: Slush still likes control, tidy invoices, and his initials on things. He's also agreed to public duties. Nib rolls up the ribbon and labels it AFTER THE TEST. Keep it handy.

missions.title: The Last Delivery Is a Question
missions.summary: Check that the city can answer back.
intro: One more trip around the city. Ask each stop: Are you ready, and who answers if you're not? Bring back actual replies. A ceremonial parcel would've been lighter.

steps.hint: Frostwick Depot: collect the launch question packet.
pages: Foreman signs: The heavy parts route stays clear. I hold the gate key and a spare at the archive. If the gate freezes, call me; do not send the load over the roof bridge. The foreman draws a very heavy arrow under this.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: inspect the launch packet mismatch at the shelf.
pages: Rivet checks a practice packet with four branch names and only three received marks. Frostwick, Candy, and Brassworks have signed. Velvet has a sent entry but no received mark. Moxie is free to carry a copy; the lamp card cannot confirm it. Pip starts to count the sent entry as close enough, catches himself, and leaves the empty box visible. Nib would rather answer a real check than be congratulated by assumption.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: record Moxie's launch reply.
pages: Moxie signs: Stops are named, signal cards posted, backup copies ready. If I miss a handoff, Pip gets the truth. She adds that the sled runner now turns without editorial comment, then crosses out now to avoid tempting fate.

steps.hint: Brassworks Foundry: record Rivet's launch reply.
pages: Rivet signs: Spring checked, limit set, seal supply recorded. If a reading disagrees with the bucket, we investigate the reading before changing the city. She gives you the wooden spoon. It has earned a place in the public tool record.

steps.hint: Candy Sorting: choose the one launch packet that needs a courier copy.
pages: Which branch should receive the backup copy in this practice packet? Do not resend every confirmed delivery just to look busy. Identify the unmatched sent entry and use the assigned backup duty. Moxie puts her finger beside the three signatures and waits for a destination, not an instruction to ride around until somebody feels reassured.
wrong: Compare branch names against received marks. Only one listed branch
has an attempted send without the confirmation required by the
launch rule.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: confirm what a missing reply means.
pages: One station has not replied to the launch question. What can the clerk honestly record as the next action?
wrong: A missing reply is neither agreement nor refusal. Use the rule for
establishing what happened instead of inventing an answer.

outro: You name the last check. The clerk signs. Every stop has a duty and a way to get help. Pip starts holding the packet like a trophy. Dot reminds him about the corners.

missions.title: What the Warmth Is For
missions.summary: Choose the network first emphasis.
intro: The network can start. The public fund can back one first emphasis; the other plans wait. All choices keep the public branches and access agreement. Pick where to begin. Nobody gets cut off.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: hear the three proposals at the festival desk.
pages: Pip proposes WARMTH: first upgrades for homes and clinic rooms. Rivet proposes INDUSTRY: first upgrades for shops that make repairs and wages. Nib proposes COMMONS: first upgrades for shared halls, kitchens, and public meeting rooms. Each includes basic service for every district.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: read the baseline and improvement budget beside the bypass.
pages: The public fund sets aside six tokens for basic service: two for homes, two for work sites, two for shared rooms. It has three more for the first improvements. One draft spends four extra tokens on a grand hall and silently takes one from the home baseline. Nib rejects that draft before anyone votes. Preferences may decide the extra three; they must not remove the common floor everyone agreed to preserve.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: inspect the common protections on the grid.
pages: Dot reads the protections aloud. Service stays within FOUR. Faults are logged. Public paths stay open. Homes are not pledged against the repair debt. Slush asks whether these apply to all three proposals. They do. He nods and puts away a fourth proposal.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: select the first service emphasis at the turbine.
pages: Choose the first emphasis. WARMTH improves daily comfort. WORK invests first in repair shops and livelihoods. COMMONS invests first in shared places. All three restore the network and keep the city open for free exploration.
outcomes: Pip marks homes and the clinic for the first upgrades. He says
comfort is useful work too. Rivet agrees and asks which window leaks
most.
Rivet marks repair shops for the first upgrades. The first wage
board includes paid training, so the work has a door people can
enter.
Nib marks the shared halls for the first upgrades. He gives up the
grand opening speech and asks who has keys to the kitchen.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: protect the common baseline before applying your emphasis.
pages: Which improvement budget can be promised without taking tokens from basic service? The same budget applies to every emphasis. It defines the honest amount any of the three proposals may spend first. Pip will read the figure before the ribbon, because an inspiring proposal is still a promise somebody must be able to keep.
wrong: Separate the six tokens already committed to the baseline from the
additional improvement fund. Only the uncommitted amount can support
the first emphasis.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: confirm the plan with Slush at the bypass.
pages: Slush checks the public protections, then signs as one participant. He has kept the old fault card. This time, he says, if my branch fails, I know who to call. Pip answers: And they know you will answer back.
Slush offers his roof crew for the first drafty homes. The clinic
gets a plain cost estimate before anyone orders a gold plaque.
Slush offers paid tool training space in the lodge yard. Rivet
insists trainees learn shutdown tests before polishing the machines.
Slush offers the lodge hall on the posted public schedule. Nib
writes its capacity honestly and leaves room for a coat rack.

outro: Your first emphasis is recorded, with the protections intact. No hidden score. Next comes the service check and festival switch. Pip's speech is down to one page. We can work with that.

missions.title: A City That Answers
missions.summary: Start service and leave the city open.
intro: The crowd includes couriers, roofers, a clerk, a foreman, and neighbors who've waited years for an answer. Small ribbon. Ordinary switch. Let's see what happens when someone uses it.

steps.hint: Aurora Signal: confirm the final received mark at the lantern.
pages: The lantern shows STEADY, and the written received card is signed. The backup courier is named in the log. Dot reads both before declaring the signal ready. Pip waits for the whole sentence, which she appreciates more than he knows. The received launch card also confirms the normal service limit is FOUR. The brief test ceiling remains SIX; EIGHT remains a damage warning. Dot asks you to carry that checked value to the final grid inspection, rather than remembering the largest number on the old plate.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: read the last combined launch check at the bypass.
pages: The final rehearsal combines two problems: the lodge branch is isolated for repair, and the relay reply is unconfirmed. Other branches remain within the service budget. The archive foot route is available for the message copy. Slush asks if the whole launch must stop. Dot says the plan has separate responses for separate faults; the important question is whether each is actually used, not whether the city can pretend the faults never happened.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: verify the launch service setting at the grid.
pages: Verify the correct normal service setting before the launch. A celebration does not change the engineering record.
wrong: The final check must use the service limit, not the brief test
ceiling or damage warning. Reopen the current mission clues if you
need the plate distinction.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: ask Rivet to start the checked turbine.
pages: Rivet fits the checked regulator, signs its launch record, and starts the turbine. The needle rises to the service mark and stays there. A branch valve clicks, then another. No one cheers until Dot confirms that the readings agree.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: choose the integrated response before the final festival report.
pages: Which combined response applies the demonstrated safeguards? HOLD means shut every branch and wait for a perfect system. PUSH means increase pressure and assume the message arrived. SERVE means keep clear branches at safe service, retain lodge isolation, and send the backup copy by the available foot route. Choose the plan you can explain to the waiting residents.
wrong: Use both safeguards together. One contains the branch problem; the
other confirms communication without relying on the failed reply
path. Neither requires denying the fault.

steps.hint: Aurora Core: join the festival at the public desk.
pages: Pip reads his speech: The city is warmer. We know why. We know what to check next. Thank you for doing your part. Nib starts the applause. Slush joins with his gloves on, then removes them so it sounds properly sincere.
The clinic hangs a handwritten list of comfortable rooms. Pip reads
every room number as if it were a grand address.
The repair shops post paid shifts beside the festival menu. Rivet
spots a typo in her title and leaves it because the wages are
correct.
The shared hall posts its first open kitchen rota. Nib has put the
cleaning duty in the same large print as the party.

outro: There's still a city to explore, jobs to take, and property to fix up. Slush keeps his umbrella. Dot keeps the pencil. Pip leaves the desk lamp on, with a blank fault form beside it. Someone will need it.

lore.title: The Unusual Index
pages: The catalog lists SNOW under WEATHER, WEATHER under OUTSIDE, and
OUTSIDE under PLEASE CLOSE THE DOOR. A newer clerk has added direct
references in neat ink. The improvement has no ribbon or donor
plaque. People now find what they came for.

lore.title: A Badge With Soup Stains
pages: The old badge has a square seal and a repaired pin. Its owner
scratched a list inside: Ask. Measure. Carry a spare. Eat lunch. The
final instruction was added more deeply than the others, perhaps
after someone learned its importance.

lore.title: The Mapmaker Eraser
pages: Along the old map edge, a route disappears beneath an eraser mark. A
note explains that the lane was removed because the stair collapsed,
not because the residents stopped mattering. A later hand restores
the route through a service hall.

lore.title: The Clerk Lunch
pages: A tin beside the clerk contains two spoons, although she works
alone. She says one is for visitors who bring a hard problem near
lunchtime. The soup is ordinary potato. The extra spoon has probably
saved more arguments than the stamp collection.

lore.title: The Missing Comma
pages: An old manifest ordered twelve crates of bells and one foreman.
Someone added a comma and a note: Foreman arrives under own power.
The foreman has framed the correction. He says accurate records
matter, particularly when the records threaten to ship him.

lore.title: The Borrowed Hammer
pages: Every tool has a numbered outline except a hammer whose place says
WITH ELSA, EAST ROOF. A return date is crossed out and replaced with
ASK IF ROOF IS SAFE. The depot can tolerate a missing hammer better
than a missing neighbor.

lore.title: The Gate Height
pages: The gate beam has tiny marks for parcel loads and three pencil marks
for a child height. The tallest child mark now has a courier license
number beside it. Moxie pretends not to recognize the handwriting.
The foreman pretends to believe her.

lore.title: A Kettle Schedule
pages: The kettle card gives names, not hours. Whoever takes the last cup
fills it. Whoever comes in cold gets the first. The foreman calls
this a scheduling system. He says its only serious defect is Pip
interpreting cold as an emotional condition.

lore.title: Bells With a Purpose
pages: The red shelf contains watch bells, door bells, and one bell labeled
NO PURPOSE YET. Moxie refuses to discard it. A useful thing can wait
for a useful job, she says. It need not become a souvenir simply
because the invoice is tidy.

lore.title: A Blanket Label
pages: A blanket tag names the person who sewed it and the person who
checked it. Neither name is large. Someone has added a third line
for whoever repairs it next. The tag assumes the blanket will live
long enough to need another kind pair of hands.

lore.title: The Address That Moved
pages: One address card reads: Mrs. Elm, formerly third floor, now ground
floor by the ramp. Her mail followed her before the official map
did. The couriers keep the correction pinned up until the city
prints a new map. Accuracy sometimes starts on a scrap.

lore.title: The Famous Racing Stripe
pages: Moxie's racing stripe is painted on the inside of the sled runner,
where almost nobody sees it. She painted it during a long repair. It
reminds her the sled can move again. She claims it adds speed, but
only when properly maintained.

lore.title: A Letter Never Sent
pages: A draft resignation sits beneath the courier ledger. It begins: I
cannot promise the impossible. The next line reads: I can promise to
report what happened. The rest of the page is blank. The draft was
kept, but no envelope was ever addressed.

lore.title: The Bird Vote
pages: Small birds have scratched the vane crossbar smooth. A notice asks
residents not to treat their facing direction as a forecast. The
birds have no duty to predict weather. Moxie added: Neither does my
left knee, despite several confident newspaper interviews.

lore.title: The Quiet Reply
pages: A maintenance note describes a bell loud enough to wake the market
and a reply wire too frail to survive the cold. The note is not
about sound. Its author wanted the sender to know someone had
listened. Dot has underlined that sentence.

lore.title: The Dry Box
pages: The parcel chest has three layers of waterproof cloth and a very
modest lock. A label explains that the contents are public records.
The lock keeps wind out rather than people. Whoever last checked the
chest left a clean cloth for the next reader.

lore.title: A Tooth Number
pages: Rivet numbers each gear tooth so damage can be described exactly.
Once, a caller said the unhappy bit near the other unhappy bit.
Rivet walked across town, fixed the gear, and returned with a
numbering punch. The caller now teaches apprentices how to use it.

lore.title: The Polished Outside
pages: The regulator casing is polished only where hands rest during
maintenance. Rivet says she has nothing against polish elsewhere.
She objects when the shine arrives before the spring. The underside
bears a small engraved promise: CLOSE SAFE, EVEN WHEN THE LIGHTS DO
NOT.

lore.title: The First Apprentice
pages: Rivet's first apprentice made a bracket backward. She kept it on the
bench and asked the apprentice to design a check that would catch
the next one. The apprentice now runs inspections. The backward
bracket still holds the instruction cards upright.

lore.title: Not Waste
pages: A shelf holds parts too worn for pressure work but still useful for
training. Each bears a clear red cross and a written TRAINING label.
Rivet would rather teach with a real failed part than let a new
worker learn failure on a live pipe.

lore.title: The Bucket
pages: The measuring bucket belonged to a painter before it served the
pump. It has honest marks inside and very dishonest decorative roses
outside. Dot checked its volume against the archive measure. Pip
suggested naming it. Dot replied that BUCKET was already admirably
clear.

lore.title: A Confident Needle
pages: The gauge face carries an old slogan: ALWAYS CERTAIN. Someone has
covered CERTAIN with CHECKED. Rivet recognizes Dot's handwriting and
says nothing. Dot recognizes Rivet's silence as permission. The
crossed out word remains visible beneath the paper, which feels like
the point.

lore.title: The Spoon
pages: A wooden spoon rests beside a drawing of the contacts. It is not a
substitute for switching off power. Rivet labeled it for moving
objects away from the desk before work begins. The spoon carries a
second warning: ALSO NOT FOR LIVE SOUP.

lore.title: The Good Pencil
pages: Dot's notebook begins with tiny letters and long apologies. Later
pages have larger diagrams and fewer apologies. The last margin
says: I can be careful and still speak first. She has drawn a small
square around the sentence, as if giving herself a badge.

lore.title: Mature Silence
pages: Nib's first draft called the lodge silence mature. His revision
calls it a symptom of the idle pump. Both drafts remain on display.
The little embarrassment helps buyers see what changed. Nib says a
correction is useful only if people can find it.

lore.title: The White Space
pages: The disclosure leaves a blank strip beside each exclusion so a
reader can ask questions. Nib once thought blank space wasted a
selling chance. Now he keeps spare pencils beside it. The most
recent question is simple: Who fixes this if you move away?

lore.title: Four Branches
pages: The junction labels name districts rather than premium tiers. The
oldest label is hand cut and slightly crooked. Behind it, a worker
wrote: Same winter on both sides of this wall. Slush has not ordered
the note removed, though he can certainly see it.

lore.title: A Smaller Bow
pages: Nib's practice notes include a dramatic bow for the end of every
tour. The latest note says: Ask if they understood the roof
estimate. Bow if appropriate. His hat still has a feather. Honesty
has not required him to become dull.

lore.title: Paper Against Wind
pages: The permit clips are brass, broad, and heavier than expected. An
inspector designed them after a roof visit ended with three pages in
a chimney. The office bought better clips instead of banning roof
inspections. A small practical triumph, recorded without a slogan.

lore.title: The Greenhouse Bill
pages: A tucked receipt records a greenhouse emergency repair. The payer is
Sterling, not Slush Estates. It predates his first property
purchase. The figure is modest beside later invoices. The bottom
says: Save what can still grow. No advertising mark accompanies the
words.

lore.title: A Real View
pages: The skylight opens onto the shared pipe chase, which Nib once
described as a secluded outlook. A buyer asked what could be seen
there. Nib answered: Three valves and my mistake. The buyer kept the
quote and asked for the actual maintenance plan.

lore.title: The Unbought Line
pages: The surveyor billed for measuring walls, not for reaching Slush's
preferred result. When asked to move a boundary on paper, she
offered to measure it again. Her second measurement agreed with the
first. The invoice includes both visits and no change of boundary.

lore.title: An Unanswered Seat
pages: Beside the signal log stands a chair with a mended cushion. The
clerk waited there after the old alarm, expecting a reply from
anyone. She still uses the chair, but now the desk has space for a
